correctness.rationale: For the repaired claim finiteness of a31 forces p(3)=1. Previously infinite supported parameters can be replaced by a common sufficiently large real (every new path exceeds the target), then the left diagonal can be gauged to zero. Bottom row and first column fix u,v,w and c,d. In 321, d1..d4≥0 follow from the available paths via the bottom row. If d2,d3>0, the only minimizing paths at (2,3) and (1,2) force y=a23 and b+x=a12 with x≥a22. Hence a13≤b+y≤a12-a22+a23, giving d5≥0. Conversely set x=a22 and z=a13. If d3=0, y=a23 and b=max(a12-a22,a13-a23) suffice because the bottom-row path already realizes a12. If d3>0, take b=a12-a22 and y=max(a23,a13-b); it either equals a23 by d5≥0 or may be increased without affecting a23 because d2=0. In 231 the sole central path gives d1=0, with the remaining three bounds necessary; taking x=a12,y=a13,z=a23,b=a13-a23 realizes all the minima. Their union and the 231-only region now follow by substitution, including boundary equalities. Both numerical examples satisfy their claimed defects and memberships. The amended Grigoriev comparison matches the original statement: k=1,s=3 admits four minors, while k=2,s=2 admits (q,m)=(1,3), giving d5. No original counterexample claim was retained.
residual_risks: The finite certificate does not prove all-real membership; the reconstructed min-plus elimination does. Targets with infinite entries and matrices of other sizes are outside scope.

value.rationale: The generic longest-cell test explicitly leaves a boundary problem. The repaired classification closes it in the first size with two possible finite cells, gives factors on both exceptional parts of the longest cell, and distinguishes decomposability in the second cell even when the longest-cell test fails. The complete criterion is useful for arbitrarily degenerate finite data and does not rely for significance on the false allegation of an error in the prior theorem.
residual_risks: No extension to arbitrary dimension or infinite target entries is asserted.
